articles.title: Top House Oversight Democrat warns Trump family to 'lawyer up'
articles.text:
Rep. Robert Garcia, the California Democrat poised to lead the powerful House Oversight Committee, doubled down on his warning to President Donald Trump and his allies Friday, releasing a video promising sweeping investigations into the administration.
"Oversight Democrats are ready to take on the crooks, the con men and the Trump crime family. Lawyer up," the California Democrat wrote on X.
"The American people have spoken, and they are tired of the unprecedented level of corruption coming out of this White House and under President Trump," Garcia said in the video, which ends with the words "LAWYER UP" splashed across the screen.
The warning comes three days after Democrats' sweeping midterm victories handed them control of the House. When the new Congress convenes in January, Democrats will gain control of the committee's subpoena power, allowing them to compel testimony and obtain documents in investigations that could target Trump, his family and his allies.
Garcia said the committee would investigate what he described as potential corruption involving the Trump family's business dealings, cryptocurrency ventures and Pentagon contracts, as well as alleged abuses by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He also vowed to scrutinize individuals he said were connected to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
"Oversight Democrats are absolutely going to ensure that we investigate every single one of these instances," Garcia said. "Now let's get to work."
Garcia's approach may conflict with what some advisors are telling Democrats — to go after corporate interests rather than Trump and his family.
Garcia, currently the committee's top Democrat, formally launched his bid to become chairman Thursday. He is widely expected to secure the position.
The White House has dismissed Democrats' planned investigations as politically motivated, setting up a potentially contentious showdown between the Trump administration and the incoming Democratic congressional majority.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

articles.title: OpenAI bugging suspect Alfozan pleads not guilty
articles.text:
The Saudi national charged with planting a listening device in the headquarters of OpenAI while he worked there pleaded not guilty on Friday during an appearance in San Francisco federal court.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was sent back to jail after the brief hearing. Alfozan has been held without bail since his arrest on a criminal complaint in early October.
He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted in the case.
A grand jury indicted Alfozan on Oct. 27 on a single count of interception of oral communications, court records show.
Prosecutors say that he put a recording device in a television in an executive conference room at OpenAI's offices in San Francisco on Sept. 28.
Alfozan's lawyer declined to comment after the hearing before Magistrate Judge Peter Kang.
The judge ordered Alfozan to next appear in court on Nov. 17.
Alfozan is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm, Raed Ventures.
"He currently serves as Engineering Lead at OpenAI, with a focus on AI Agents and the data platform," Alfozan's bio page on Raed's site says.
Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, a member of Saudi Arabia's royal family, is a venture partner in the same firm.
Alfozan's case comes as U.S. companies such as OpenAI are making rapid advancements in developing artificial intelligence agents, and as concerns grow about the potential theft of AI tech from those companies.
In June, President Donald Trump, in an executive order on AI innovation, said it was U.S. policy "to protect American ingenuity and intellectual property from exploitation and theft by adversaries; and to cultivate America's advanced AI-enabled capabilities."
Trump has had a close relationship with Saudi Arabia. But he has also taken steps during his second term in the White House to limit the number of visas for highly skilled foreign workers.
OpenAI earlier this year held discussions with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the country's sovereign wealth fund, about investing in the company.
— Jordan Novet reported from San Francisco

articles.title: A disturbing employment trend is hiding beneath the latest strong job numbers
articles.text:
Americans who lose their jobs these days are facing a harsh new problem: It's getting harder to find another one quickly.
The average jobless worker's bout of unemployment surpassed 27 weeks in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, according to Friday's jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That amounts to a job search of nearly seven months, the longest outside of the pandemic period since 2016, when the U.S. labor market was finally getting back on track after the 2008 financial crisis.
About 2 million Americans have been without work for at least 27 weeks, the BLS reported. People in this category are referred to as the "long-term unemployed" and accounted for 27.6% of all jobless workers in October, the highest share since late 2021.
"This is a series that can be noisy from month to month," said Cory Stahle, senior economist at Indeed, a hiring platform. "But if you look over a longer time horizon, there is no mistake in the trend."
It's a troubling sign in an otherwise steady labor market. Workers stuck on the sidelines are a casualty of what's become a "low-hire, low-fire" job market, in which companies are hesitant to lay workers off, but aren't adding them either.
Research shows that Americans who experience long-term unemployment face depleted savings, lower earnings potential over time and declining mental health.
What's more, workers who are unemployed for extended periods risk falling into a self-perpetuating cycle, researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond wrote earlier this year.
"Time spent unemployed may itself reduce the probability of finding a job, perhaps because skills depreciate, networks thin or employers interpret long unemployment durations as a negative signal," the researchers warned.
Workers stop being able to claim most, if not all, government unemployment benefits after 26 weeks in a year. Given that, a rising share of long-term unemployed people can explain in part why initial and continuing jobless claims have remained low.
"Now, the average unemployed person takes longer to find a job than their benefits would last," Stahle said. "That is a really key point of this."
A 'jarring' narrative
While jobless workers appear to be having a tough time, this week's employment data shows strength in other areas of the labor market.
Nonfarm payrolls blew past economists' forecasts for October and added 165,000 jobs, according to Friday's release. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%, slightly lower than economists predicted.
Job openings came in much higher than economists expected in September, according to a separate report from the BLS released on Tuesday. The number of workers quitting jobs — a barometer of their confidence to obtain new employment — spiked to levels not seen since March 2025.
The BLS also said layoffs and discharges dropped to their lowest volume in more than a year. However, a recent string of high-profile workforce cuts could throw cold water on views among workers that the market is heating up.
CNBC reported this week that Disney is planning to axe thousands of jobs, the latest of several waves of layoffs at the media giant this year. American Express said last month that it was slashing head count by 5% as it reorients around artificial intelligence.
"It's difficult to separate what's happening to you or the people around you from the big picture," said Elizabeth Renter, lead economist at Life360. "When your LinkedIn is filled with layoffs and your social circle features a few folks who have been job seeking for several months, positive narratives about the labor market can seem jarring."

articles.title: Trump says Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff
articles.text:
President Donald Trump on Friday announced White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller will be promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.
Trump revealed the stunning shake-up just three days after Democrats won a landslide victory in the midterm elections, gaining majority control in the House and Senate and scrambling the trajectory of Trump's last two years in office.
Elevating Miller, an architect of Trump's controversial mass-deportation efforts, is bound to raise the hackles of the incoming class of congressional Democrats, who have already vowed to investigate the government's immigration policies.
"It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have served on his team from Day One, and I am honored beyond words to serve as his White House Chief of Staff," Miller said on X later Friday.
"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic," he said.
Miller will take over starting Monday, Trump said in a Truth Social post, praising his longtime aide as "one of my most trusted advisors."
Wiles, "who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation," the president wrote.
Asked about the move later Friday afternoon, Trump said, "I wanted to make a change."
"I think Susie's done a very good job, great job. But I just wanted to make it," Trump told reporters as he left the White House for an event in Cape Canaveral, Florida.
"Stephen's been great," Trump said, adding, "Sometimes in life you have to make moves."
Wiles resigned Thursday night, a senior White House source told MS NOW. Wiles told Trump, who was said to be angry with her following the GOP's huge election losses, "let me make this easy on you — I am going to resign," MS NOW reported.
"Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff," Wiles said in an X post Friday afternoon. "Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime."
"While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will," she wrote.
Senior administration officials were quick to congratulate Miller.
"Patriots in control," read an X post from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose job security has come into question after some Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, blamed the midterm results on the Iran war.
Vance also praised Miller on X, saying he "will do great things."
The official X account for Trump's political operation celebrated the announcement by posting a black-and-white photo of Miller under the caption, "It's Miller time."
Democrats and other critics, meanwhile, filed in to denounce the pick.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who could be elected House speaker next year, called Miller "a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands."
"His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today," Jeffries wrote on X.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., wrote that Trump "learned nothing from his historic defeat."
"Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn't have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way," Schumer wrote.
Others took Miller's promotion as a sign that Trump, who seemed to express some willingness to negotiate with a blue Congress, will instead remain combative.
"For those who hoped the @POTUS might pivot to work with the incoming Congress, the appointment of Miller is a bucket of ICE cold water," wrote David Axelrod, a former senior advisor to President Barack Obama.
The White House reshuffle follows multiple resignations of senior staff in the Department of Justice since Election Day. They include Harmeet Dhillon, a leader in the DOJ's civil rights division, John Eisenberg, who headed the national security division, and Jason Reding Quiñones, who had been in charge of conspiracy investigations related to Trump's foes.
Wiles oversaw Trump's winning 2024 presidential campaign and has wielded major influence in his second administration, while largely staying out of the spotlight. She drew focus in late 2025, when Vanity Fair reported that Wiles admitted that Trump had pursued "retribution" as president and that he had an "alcoholic's personality."
Trump, and many other top administration officials, defended Wiles at the time, underscoring her status in the White House.
While Wiles is not fully leaving Trump's orbit, her resignation follows a pattern of other top female officials who have left or been fired from Trump's second administration, and then replaced by men.

articles.title: Fake job interview scams like the one that hit Binance are getting more sophisticated. Here are the new signs to watch for
articles.text:
Job search scams can cost applicants hundreds or thousands of dollars. But one fake job interview recently impacted over $6 billion in assets.
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, announced on Tuesday it recently experienced a security breach impacting $6.34 billion in digital assets. The hack was enabled in part by a job seeker's nightmare: bogus job interviews.
While the Binance hackers had their sights set on a much bigger target than an individual job seeker, job-related scams are on the rise. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) tallied employment-related losses amounting to roughly $363 million in 2025, up sharply from $264 million the year prior, and $70 million in 2023. The actual figure is likely higher, since many victims of such crimes do not report them.
Those orchestrating fake job scams have many potential targets today "because the job search is taking so long for so many right now," says Stefanie Fackrell, a former recruiter at Google and Nvidia. While October's jobs report showed promise as the U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs, far more than expected, many applicants have been struggling through a low-hire, low-fire market for months.
"With today's job market, people are anxious, they're tired, many are at their wits' end," says Leeza Garber, a privacy and cybersecurity expert and adjunct law professor at Drexel University's Kline School of Law. "A proactive inquiry can be something you just immediately respond to without thinking."
Artificial intelligence can also make scams more widespread and harder to detect.
"Cyber scams in general are becoming much more sophisticated just because they're evolving at the same speed as AI and public access to AI," says Garber. "AI is going to make things seem more and more real."
In 2025, victims reported losses of almost $13 million to AI-involved employment scams, according to the IC3.
What happened in the Binance hack
Binance's announcement included an abbreviated play-by-play of how its hack went down. Fackrell and Garber broke down some of the warning signs in how the events unfolded, including what job seekers can learn from the incident.
What happened: A software engineer, who was not named, was contacted through "a legitimate job-hunting platform" by someone posing as a project director, Binance said in its announcement. That person arranged for the engineer to have an initial interview with a purported HR representative and a second-round interview with the supposed CEO of a fake company.
Experts' red flags: A headshot that's clearly AI-generated or otherwise looks uncanny, as well as sparse profile information or activity, and few connections should give you pause, Fackrell says. On LinkedIn, for example, you can click the three dots on a person's profile to open an "About this member" pop-up, where you can see when they joined LinkedIn and if they've verified their identity, workplace and school.
Though some small startups may arrange for an interview with a C-suite executive, it's generally unusual, particularly for a second-round interview, unless you'd be reporting to that person, she adds.
What happened: In the first round, the fake HR representative had a live video interview with the software engineer, even sharing with him a social media account with personal photos and videos to build trust, Binance said. The tactic was "more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches," Binance added in its announcement.
Experts' red flags: A recruiter might bring up commonalities with a candidate like the same alma mater or ex-employer to "bring that human element into the conversation," Fackrell says. But sharing personal social media in a first-round interview is strange, she adds.
In video interviews in general, some red flags might include the person moving unusually slowly or not responding to one of your questions, or their visual skipping a beat, Garber says.
What happened: The second-round interview with the purported CEO of the fake company was conducted on "a popular social chat app," Binance said, and the software engineer was instructed to download "an 'assignment' containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer."
Experts' red flags: Interviews commonly happen over Microsoft Teams, Zoom or Google Meet, not a social chat app. "I don't know anybody that's FaceTiming or WhatsApping any of their candidates," Fackrell says.
While take-home assignments, particularly for technical roles, may use third-party systems, don't download software if you're not familiar with it, Fackrell advises. These assignments should be shared via email through a legitimate system, not over the phone. Job seekers should take interviews on a personal device, not a work computer.
Tips to avoid job search scams
Common job search scams today include:
- A fake recruiter reaching out to someone about a position and asking for their resume, only to say their resume must be rewritten, for a fee, to be considered
- Extending a fake job offer and asking the recipient to pay for job equipment, including by cashing a fake check to cover it and sending back "excess" funds; or asking the recipient to provide sensitive information, such as ID, bank account details, or Social Security number
- Text messages offering jobs that seem too easy, such as being paid to like social media content or leave positive reviews, as scammers typically ask these workers for their own money down the line
Job sites like LinkedIn and Indeed, and entities like the Federal Trade Commission and Better Business Bureau, also have more information about common scams.
You should not have to provide sensitive information or payment in order to get a job, according to the FTC. Legitimate recruiters will reach out from their corporate email addresses, not a personal address. Other red flags include pressure to move quickly through the hiring process or seeing multiple typos in communications.
"Do your research before clicking, responding or engaging with anybody," Fackrell says.
Take a minute to think about how you were contacted and what you're being asked to do to proceed, Garber suggests, and cross-check job postings against the company's official careers page.
"If seems too good to be true, it definitely is," says Garber.

articles.title: Americans are on a 'treadmill of high inflation' and more rate hikes are likely, Fed's Daly says
articles.text:
San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly said Friday she expects the central bank will need to raise interest rates further, but joined her fellow policymakers in saying the pace and timing remain uncertain.
"My expectation is we're going to have to tighten policy further. Exactly when and how much is still to be decided because we just have to take all the variables that are coming in," Daly told CNBC's Steve Liesman during a live interview. "More is likely to be needed, and certainly ... I'm prepared to do that if that's what the economy calls for."
The remarks came the same day the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October while the unemployment rate — the labor-market variable Fed officials focus on most — edged lower to 4.1%.
Those numbers were substantially better than Wall Street expectations. Job creation, in fact, was nearly triple the Dow Jones consensus estimate.
Daly called the report "good news for American workers," but noted the pressure inflation is exerting on household finances. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% annually in October, but the September inflation rate as measured by the consumer price index was 3.7%.
"They see that they can get jobs, they continue to spend. They're not out of the game, but they are on a treadmill of high inflation," she said. "This has been high for too long, almost six years, and we're really starting to feel the burden of that spread everywhere."
The policymaker said she's not concerned generally about economic growth but worried about the persistence of inflation.
"The job market remains stable and solid, but not booming, and you see real wages falling because those wages are not really keeping up with inflation," Daly said. "I think that's the crux of this. Good news on the jobs front, not so clear that Americans are going to gain ground in the labor market."
The rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee in September increased the central bank's benchmark overnight borrowing rate by a quarter percentage point to a target range of 3.75%-4%.
However, the committee last week declined to follow up that hike with another move, saying it preferred to wait for "the accumulation of more information" before deciding its next move.
Daly will vote on the committee next year and said she still favors a gradual approach. Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin said Thursday he also sees higher rates ahead but is unsure of the timeline.
"I was really supportive and completely thought that that was the right move to move in September," Daly said. "I also think that it was good to be on hold at the last meeting because the world is filled with uncertainty."

articles.title: Microsoft plans to use fewer neoclouds as AI buildout shows signs of strain
articles.text:
Microsoft is shrinking its roster of neocloud partners as it focuses on work with a few key suppliers and builds out its own data centers, according to people familiar with the matter.
The software giant's plans pose another potential challenge for a corner of the artificial intelligence market that's showing signs of strain due to rising borrowing costs, hefty debt loads and concerns about whether the buildout will slow down.
Microsoft has forged relationships in recent years with a number of neoclouds, including CoreWeave, Nebius, Chronoscale, IREN, Lambda and Nscale, as well as with Oracle, which is pouring money into building out AI infrastructure.
Microsoft is now in the evaluation stage and hasn't decided which neoclouds it will stop using, said two sources, who asked not to be named because the talks are confidential. One of the people said Microsoft wants to prioritize its own data center footprint. Bloomberg reported on the plans earlier. Two people said that Microsoft opted not to renew a deal with Oracle.
A Microsoft spokesperson said in an emailed statement that its infrastructure strategy is "built on flexibility and choice."
"We combine Microsoft-owned datacenters, leased facilities and strategic partnerships with third-party providers to deliver the capacity our customers need, where and when they need it," the spokesperson said. "We regularly review these investments against customer demand. That includes tracking delivery and adjusting plans as circumstances change."
The neoclouds have been a turbulent trade on Wall Street in recent weeks as rising interest rates added to fears that many companies have become overly reliant on debt in rushing to build capacity. Shares of CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all down by roughly half over the past month even after rallying on Friday.
A recent industry review counted 323 neoclouds, and experts have predicted that many of them won't survive.
In its earnings report on Thursday, IREN said it handed over data center capacity to Microsoft in August, but Microsoft requested a networking equipment upgrade that will result in the infrastructure coming online in January or February instead of this year.
Microsoft finance chief Amy Hood said on the software company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call in October that some cloud contracts involving graphics processing units were delayed until the first half of 2027, affecting Azure cloud growth. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the latest quarter, and said capex spending will accelerate in the second half of the fiscal year.
Capital markets 'more selective'
CoreWeave and Nebius are both scheduled to report quarterly results next week. IREN shares popped 16% on Friday after the company said AI revenue more than doubled from the prior quarter to $200 million. IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts told CNBC that there's a "disconnect between what we're seeing in public market and what we're seeing at the customer level."
However, he acknowledged the challenge that market conditions present.
"Capital markets have become more selective in the last few weeks, and the questions have undoubtedly moved from how big the contract is to whether it can be delivered, financed, and run at a profit," Roberts said on the earnings call.
Microsoft has already slashed its work with U.K.-based neocloud Nscale, walking away from a site that it had intended to use in England. Darren Hardman, Microsoft's CEO for the U.K and Ireland, told CNBC in October that the decision had to do with Nscale's ability to get access to electricity.
The Financial Times reported this week that Microsoft decided against renewing a contract with Nscale in Texas. Nscale filed to go public in mid-September but hasn't updated its prospectus since then. The company said in its IPO filing that it expects Microsoft to be a "significant customer in future periods."
Microsoft's big turn to neoclouds came after the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, which led to a surge in demand for GPUs. In looking elsewhere, Microsoft signed up CoreWeave, which was a privately held startup at the time with roots in cryptocurrency mining. When CoreWeave went public last year, it said 62% of its 2024 revenue came from Microsoft.
At the time of ChatGPT's release, OpenAI only used Azure. Now the company's cloud suppliers also include Amazon, Cerebras, CoreWeave, Google and Oracle.
Microsoft's spokesperson said that its approach to reviewing neocloud investments is "a normal and responsible way to manage large, complex infrastructure projects," and that "the pace of our new agreements reflects what we need today."
—CNBC's Kif Leswing contributed to this report.

articles.title: OpenAI, Arm and Qualcomm executives react to post-midterm AI sell-off
articles.text:
As a post-midterm rally Wednesday turned into a steep sell-off Thursday, tech executives sought to look through the notion that potential data center constraints could be catastrophic for their businesses.
In response to a Democratic sweep of Congress as well as a sizeable number of state governorships and legislatures in the midterm election Tuesday night, stocks initially rallied Wednesday, posting their best day in more than 18 months as President Trump accepted the blowout results with little fanfare.
The tide quickly turned Thursday, however, with stocks selling off sharply as investors feared a potential slowdown in the data center build-out after wins by candidates in favor of data center regulation in states like Texas and the possibility that the artificial intelligence trade may be past its peak. Tech led the sell-off, with the "Magnificent Seven" losing over $1 trillion in aggregate market cap.
Stocks recovered some of their losses Friday.
Here's how tech executives reacted to the midterms and sell-off threat:
Arm CEO Rene Haas
Haas characterized the postelection fear as "very, very short term thinking" and not likely to be a major threat to Arm's business in the long term, but said the U.S. must keep investing in the data center build-out before the rest of the world catches up.
"If the U.S. hesitates in any way, shape, or form in terms of data center build-out, the rest of the world is ready and willing. There is just huge demand for this capacity," Haas told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Thursday.
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar
Friar told CNBC's Sara Eisen Friday that OpenAI will continue investing in data center infrastructure after voters resoundly rejected data centers in their backyards during the midterm election. The company will also focus on community concerns, including electricity. "We will never raise your electricity bill," Friar said.
"When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand.  It starts early with having built relationships with all of the hyperscalers, and it will continue to mean that we raise capital," Friar said.
"If the midterm means more focus on data centers and communities, we're going to keep doing the work to get into those communities and to build trust with them."
Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon
Amon said the anxiety about the future of the data center build-out doesn't pose a significant threat to the chipmaker's business, as data center infrastructure is just one segment. Qualcomm slid 9.49% in Thursday's sell-off before recovering some losses Friday.
"The whole market is down, but I think the Qualcomm story is a little bit different," Amon told CNBC's Jon Fortt Thursday. Unlike traditional PC and data center chipmakers, Qualcomm has historically focused on low-power consumption computing. "The story of Qualcomm is what we have done outside that on the data center specific question."
Box CEO Aaron Levie
Levie told "Squawk on the Street" Thursday that productivity gains meant AI "is clearly going in one direction," but said a tendency for industry messaging to coalesce around "doomerism" can exacerbate the public perception problems AI companies face.
"I think it's a little bit easier to rotate it toward maybe the more risk-oriented messages, and that's something that our industry needs to work on clearly. But ultimately, obviously, the consumer needs to see the direct benefit, and that's something that will just take time," said Box's Levie.
Lyft CEO David Risher
Risher said the dour market sentiment wasn't concerning for Lyft's business, as consumer sentiment and bookings remained strong. 
"I wouldn't get too distracted about the short term stuff of what's going on in the market. If I look at the consumer, for example, we just had the biggest Halloween we've ever had," Risher told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Friday.

articles.title: AI crush is powering one stock to sky-high valuations
articles.text:
The 2026 midterm elections have profoundly altered the national regulatory environment, most notably with Democrats securing control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress and notching big victories in traditionally business-friendly states like Texas and South Carolina.
Over the past two decades, Southern states like Florida and Texas have attracted massive corporate migration from blue states. With less regulation and lower taxes. Those same benefits also attracted many people seeking lower taxes, lower housing costs, and better economic opportunities. With this political shift, relocated companies may now face a landscape increasingly focused on energy and building constraints, and tighter legislative oversight.
Information technology, semiconductors, and traditional energy sectors experienced immediate headwinds following the election. Companies at the forefront of the AI boom, such as CoreWeave, Tesla, and SpaceX, saw share prices slide as markets priced in tighter Democratic regulatory oversight and potential restrictions on AI deployment. Senator Bernie Sanders, for example, reposted his efforts to advance a data center moratorium proposal he co-authored with New York Congresswoman and socialist Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
The market is suddenly realizing that, between shifts in Washington and in states like Texas, the fastest-growing area of the U.S. economy might grind to a halt. Over half of the U.S. hyperscale data center pipeline could now face heightened regulatory friction. To build new facilities, even assuming they get permitted at all, developers may face tax increases, strict "bring your own power" mandates, or new air-permit delays for on-site gas plants. As all-in construction costs rise and timelines extend, immediate demand for advanced chips snowballs down the hardware supply chain.
Traditional oil and gas majors sank, while solar and green energy stocks surged, driven by expectations that a Democratic Congress will resume pushing subsidies for them. Also, the ongoing U.S.-Israel war with Iran has driven crude prices sharply higher throughout the year. With Democrats taking control of Congress, President Trump faces a legislative body that can severely constrain his military options and push back on defense budgets. Tehran almost certainly recognized that a politically weakened Trump administration would have a greater incentive to seek a negotiated deal, something Secretary of State Marco Rubio has now indicated is preferable to any escalating kinetic options. Consequently, crude prices plunged, with Brent dropping below $95 per barrel.
For similar reasons, defense contractors took market hits due to anticipated congressional resistance to the $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget. Although healthcare - as measured by XLV at least came in today, it remains above pre-election levels, along with grocery stocks such as Walmart, Costco, Kroger, and Dollar General, on expectations that a Democratic Congress might boost federal spending in those areas.
This may help explain why Costco was one of the relatively few stocks to close higher on Thursday, and why it also ranked as the 15th most active single-stock option (in notional terms), ahead of names like JP Morgan, Marvell, Oracle, Eli Lilly, and Dell.
At roughly 46x forward earnings, Costco (a perennial on the "Holly Index (MELLOY, CAN WE LINK TO THIS") isn't cheap, but then it is never cheap. The average forward multiple is actually a few turns higher at over 49x. So what were folks trading? Mostly short-dated call options. One possible reason? Costco isn't just trading at a relatively high multiple; as usual, it is also simply a high-priced stock in dollar terms, at over $1,065 as of Thursday's close. A "round lot" (100 shares) would therefore cost over $100,000 to initiate. Like many things packaged at Costco, that might be a little more than some buyers need (or want) to spend.
Alternatively, call options let investors gain exposure to 100 shares for far less than buying the shares. Buying the January 1060 calls, for example, would cost about $53.45, or $5,345 for upside participation on 100 shares of stock above the $1,060 strike price. That may seem more palatable, but a keen observer might notice that prior highs occasionally present some technical resistance, and Costco topped out at about $1,090 back in mid-May. By selling a call at or near that level, such as the January 1090s at 39.65, one could reduce the cost of the trade even further, expecting a pause before new highs. This would reduce the cost of the trade to $13.80, or just under 1.3% of the current stock price.
I won't pretend $1,380 is a small outlay for a one-lot call spread on a much-loved stock trading at 46x forward earnings. Nor is $520 for 8 6-ounce A5 Wagyu filet mignons (a Costco online only deal available now). But relatively, both the steaks at Costco and the options on Costco are very fairly priced. But it does provide participation in 100 shares of Costco between the strikes, for only 30% more than the cost of a single share of the underlying stock.

articles.title: Mississippi Senate: Longshot Ty Pinkins says he aimed to spoil Hyde-Smith, boost Colom vote
articles.text:
Longshot Mississippi Senate candidate Ty Pinkins said that at first wanted to win — but that he stayed in to spoil.
Pinkins told a local TV station that after an April poll showed he had no chance of winning he remained in the race in order to boost Democratic nominee Scott Colom's chances of beating Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Pinkins' purported strategy might pay off.
Colom is narrowly leading Hyde-Smith in ongoing counting by just 1,936 votes, a margin of just 0.2 percentage points, with 96.2% of the vote counted, according to the Associated Press. That margin is about one-tenth the size of Pinkins' share of the vote, 2.1 percentage points.
Pinkins has won just 20,010 votes so far out of the nearly 952,000 votes already counted.
"The only thing I did was stay in the race and let people shoot arrows at me," Pinkins said in an interview with WTVA in Mississippi on Thursday. "That is it. And that's a ... low price to pay to get someone in this race that I think can help people in the Delta and all across this state."
"The portion of the vote that I drew — and people were concerned about splitting the Black vote — what I actually did was split the Republican vote," he said.
Pinkins told the station in Tupelo that he intentionally avoided campaigning in areas with large Black populations to avoid cutting into the vote share of Colom, who, like Pinkins, is Black.
That tactic worked, he said, as the election results show he got most of his support from areas with relatively low Black populations.
"I'll be the boogeyman," he said. "But I'll tell you this: The independent in this race pulled most of his votes from a Republican, and for the first time since Reconstruction, a Democrat who is a Black man is leading."
Pinkins, a lawyer who previously ran for Mississippi secretary of state, was the Democratic nominee for Senate in 2024. He was crushed by Republican Sen. Roger Wicker, who won nearly 63% of the vote, compared with about 37% for Pinkins.
Despite that showing, the U.S. Army veteran decided to take another crack at the Senate in 2026.
But in the spring, he saw the writing on the wall for his candidacy.
"I got in this race to win," Pinkins told WTVA. "In April, I knew I was going to lose, but I also knew that I was pulling 70% of the Republican vote based on the [SPLC Action Fund and Impact Research] poll."
SPLC Action Fund, when it released the poll, said, "Sagging favorability numbers for Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith could open up a path to victory for Democrats."
"Independent Ty Pinkins has the potential to play spoiler for either candidate," SPLC Action Fund said in April.
In the WTVA interview, Pinkins said, "I probably attended maybe, maybe six events over the summer" as part of his campaign.
"Six events. I don't have to," Pinkins said. "Why? I'm not going to win. So why go to these Black communities that he's going to?"
Pinkins said all he had to do was visit counties that have relatively low Black populations and "talk to some Republicans that said they're going to vote for me."
"They were literally calling me and sending me emails: 'We're going to vote for you because we don't want to waste our vote on Cindy Hyde-Smith, we don't want to hold our nose and vote for her, so we're going to vote for you. Please stay in the race,'" he said.
The campaigns of Colom and Hyde-Smith did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

articles.title: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: Nvidia, Moderna, IonQ, Airbnb, Firefly Aerospace & more
articles.text:
Market Insider
Stocks making the biggest moves midday: Nvidia, Moderna, IonQ, Airbnb, Firefly Aerospace & more
Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. IonQ – The quantum computing stock rose 17% after IonQ lifted its full-year guidance for revenue. The company sees revenue in a range of $505 million to $515 million, topping analysts' estimate for $456.2 million, per FactSet. Firefly Aerospace – The company announced a roughly $1.3 billion agreement with AST SpaceMobile in which it will provide 36 rocket engines and a license to the engine's intellectual property. Firefly surged nearly 30%, while AST SpaceMobile advanced 6%. Microchip Technology – The semiconductor manufacturer tumbled 14% on the back of largely disappointing guidance for the current quarter. Microchip Technology sees third-quarter non-GAAP earnings ranging from 87 cents to 95 cents per share and revenue between $1.573 billion to $1.638 billion. The FactSet consensus estimate called for 94 cents a share and $1.63 billion. Moderna — The vaccine maker rallied 7%. The company smashed third-quarter earnings estimates and raised its outlook for full-year sales growth. Moderna now expects 2026 revenue growth of 15% to 25%, up from previous guidance of no more than 10%. Lam Research — The semiconductor equipment maker surged nearly 9% after the board authorized a $25 billion stock buyback . Five9 — The cloud-based contact-center-as-a-service provider fell more than 17%. Five9 lowered full-year adjusted EPS guidance and announced a $325 million cash acquisition of Level AI. Axon Enterprise — The Taser maker dropped 18% after third-quarter EPS and revenue missed Wall Street estimates, fourth-quarter guidance was weak and it pledged an additional $1.2 billion investment in drone maker Skydio, raising its stake to about 37%. Artificial intelligence and semiconductor stocks — Micron Technology, Sandisk , Marvell Technology, Advanced Micro Devices , Nebius and CoreWeave climbed Friday, recovering ground after Thursday's sharp sell-off amid concerns over potential constraints on AI data-center expansion. Nvidia rebounded more than 3% and returned to positive territory for 2026. Cloudflare — Shares climbed about 12% after guidance for the current quarter topped Street expectations. Cloudflare forecast adjusted earnings of 43 cents a share versus the LSEG consensus for 38 cents, on revenue of $845 million to $846 million, higher than analysts' consensus of $798 million. Iren – The neocloud provider jumped 19% after fiscal first-quarter revenue of $228 million grew from $137 million the prior quarter. More than $4 billion in annual recurring revenue projected to arrive in 2026 has been delayed until at least January 2027. Iren has been battered in the latest rout of AI-focused stocks, dropping 31% in the past week. Airbnb — The online lodging marketplace jumped 11% after third-quarter earnings of $3.16 per share topped analysts' consensus estimate of $2.85. Revenue of $4.87 billion beat the Street's $4.75 billion estimate, LSEG data showed. Atlassian — Shares dropped more than 14% after the supplier of team collaboration and productivity software showed year-over-year data center revenue growth expected to decline approximately 14% in the fiscal second quarter ending in December, and 16% in the fiscal year ending next June. JFrog — The software company soared 35% after raising full-year guidance. JFrog sees adjusted earnings ranging from $1.14 to $1.16 per share on revenue of $680 million to $682 million. The outlook trounced FactSet consensus estimates of 98 cents a share and $651.9 million. DraftKings — The online sports betting platform tumbled 27%. DraftKings posted a wider-than-expected third-quarter loss of 94 cents per share, worse than the 39 cent loss analysts polled by LSEG anticipated. Revenue of $1.33 billion fell short of the $1.40 billion estimate. Sportsbook revenue totaled $784 million, missing the $811.8 million StreetAccount consensus estimate. Lyft — The ridesharing company fell almost 5%. Third-quarter revenue of $1.82 billion trailed the FactSet consensus among analysts for $1.92 billion, while fourth-quarter guidance for bookings came in at $5.74 billion to $5.94 billion versus the FactSet consensus of $5.81 billion. — CNBC's Nick Wells, Darla Mercado and Scott Schnipper contributed reporting

articles.title: The AI ‘credit card’ is getting costlier as CoreWeave bond yield tops 16%
articles.text:
Debt markets are sending a message to AI data center builders: we're hiking the interest rate on your credit card and may put some new curbs on your credit limit.
That analogy comes courtesy of Jefferies global head of equity strategy, Christopher Wood, who put it in a note on Friday: "The most plausible way the AI capex arms race will end is that the credit card will be taken away."
That isn't happening yet, but credit markets have been spooked by the new political landscape — seeing more hurdles to data centers under Democratic governors in key states, along with a Democratic-controlled Congress.
The poster child for debt stress is neocloud Coreweave. The yield on its 2032 bond with a 9.625% coupon has climbed above 16%. Coreweave's five-year credit default swaps spiked above 1,289 basis points on Thursday, widening above their October peak, according to Deutsche Bank. The CDS eased 8% Friday to around 1,155.
"We've had plenty of warnings from the credit space," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note on Friday. Debt and equities are now moving more in sync, he added, "so we'll have to see if credit goes any further."
Investors are demanding more compensation to insure against default among even companies with the strongest balance sheets and credit ratings, including Nvidia, Broadcom, and Amazon.com.
CDS on Nvidia debt is up 76% in the last month. Broadcom's CDS is up 49%, while Amazon's has gained 44%. Their CDS remain low on an absolute basis; Nvidia's spread stood at roughly 139 basis points, compared with about 298 bps for Oracle and roughly 1,100 for CoreWeave. A large increase from a low starting point does not imply the same credit risk.
Still, rising CDS are a sign that markets want more protection against default among even the largest and healthiest debt issuers. And rising CDS imply higher financing costs down the line.
The market is now grappling with the prospect that at least some data center spending will be delayed or scrapped under incoming Democratic governors in Ohio, Texas, and Georgia, the three states with much of the planned capacity.
Moratoriums could impact 45% of planned capacity in the U.S. with a large amount of that in Texas, according to Goldman Sachs. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she's not opposed to data centers but wants a moratorium until the state legislature passes protections for communities.
None of these means AI debt financing is collapsing. Goldman tallies five AI bond deals totaling $67 billion since October 29, pushing total hyperscaler debt issuance this year to $296 billion. Goldman forecasts $440 billion of hyperscaler debt issuance next year, plus an additional $300 billion of project-level issuance across investment-grade and high-yield.
The Trump administration is vowing to support data centers. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told CNBC on Friday that he expects data center growth to continue as forecast, despite Democrats' big election wins.
What comes next
The big question now is how quickly AI spending will generate enough cash for hyperscalers to keep investors comfortable with future capex plans. For the neoclouds, any sign of consolidation or retrenchment in capex could result in fewer or shorter contracts for data center compute or delays in prepayments.
Goldman analysts said hyperscalers collectively reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter as capital spending exceeded operating cash flow.
"Delayed monetization and growth in purchase commitments—which we view as additional and sizable uses of cash, separate from Capex—are the key risks to more debt issuance, subject to market conditions," according to the bank.
Peak AI debt issuance may now be closer at hand. Bank of America analysts estimates that AI-related credit issuance will rise 31% from 2026 to 2027, hitting $685 billion, including public and private debt. They then see it falling 23% to $531 billion in 2028.
As for the risk? "Downside to these forecasts exists from a potential slowdown in AI infrastructure projects on the back of the Blue Wave, which will reduce capex needs and thus debt market funding," BofA said in a note.
-CNBC's Nick Wells and Michael Bloom contributed reporting

articles.title: Xuất hiện trai đẹp lai Việt - Mỹ SN 2004 vừa ra sân đã gây sốt, dân tình liền réo tên Đình Bắc
articles.text:
Xuất hiện trai đẹp lai Việt - Mỹ SN 2004 vừa ra sân đã gây sốt, dân tình liền réo tên Đình Bắc
Nam cầu thủ này sở hữu ngoại hình điển trai, khoảnh khắc trên sân thi đấu nhanh chóng gây chú ý.
V-League mùa giải 2026/2027 đang diễn ra với sự góp mặt của 14 CLB. Bên cạnh những diễn biến chuyên môn trên sân cỏ, các cầu thủ cũng trở thành tâm điểm chú ý trên mạng xã hội nhờ ngoại hình, phong cách và những câu chuyện bên lề.
Mới đây, một đoạn clip ghi lại hình ảnh một cầu thủ tại sân Yên Việt, Bắc Ninh bất ngờ thu hút sự chú ý trên mạng xã hội. Sở hữu làn da trắng, gương mặt điển trai và vóc dáng cao ráo, nam cầu thủ nhanh chóng gây chú ý dù không phải là cái tên quá quen thuộc với khán giả bóng đá Việt Nam. Chủ nhân đoạn clip còn xếp Reece ở vị trí "top 2 đẹp trai V-League" năm nay. Vừa ra sân, cậu bạn này đã được nhiều người chú ý, không ít khán giả đến xem xin chụp hình, chữ ký. Netizen xem qua màn hình cũng ấn tượng với visual của nam cầu thủ trẻ này.
Nhiều người nhanh chóng truy tìm info nam cầu thủ nêu trên. Được biết, anh chàng có tên Reece Minh-Kai, hiện hiện đang khoác áo CLB Bắc Ninh. Theo hồ sơ đăng ký cầu thủ trên trang chủ VPF, Reece Minh-Kai sinh ngày 13/10/2004, mang quốc tịch Mỹ, cao 1,73 m, nặng 70 kg và thi đấu ở vị trí tiền vệ. Anh là cầu thủ mang hai dòng máu Việt - Mỹ, có bố là người Mỹ và mẹ là người Việt Nam. Hiện tại, Reece đang khoác áo CLB Bắc Ninh với số áo 19 tại V-League 2026/2027.
Gương mặt mới này nhanh chóng nhận về nhiều lời khen ngợi của cư dân mạng: "Đẹp trai thế", "Bữa tui đi coi cũng để ý ông này, sáng bừng nha", "Tính ra bóng đá nước mình nhiều người giỏi mà đẹp", "Cứ như nam thần, mẫu ảnh",...
Tuy nhiên, điều thú vị là bên cạnh những bình luận khen ngợi Reece Minh-Kai, nhiều người cũng nhắc đến Đình Bắc. Bởi cả 2 đều sinh năm 2004. Hơn nữa, thời gian gần đây Đình Bắc đang là một trong những gương mặt nổi bật của lứa cầu thủ trẻ Việt Nam, không chỉ nhờ phong độ thi đấu mà còn bởi sức hút trên mạng xã hội. Sở hữu gương mặt điển trai, chiều cao hơn 1m80 cùng những khoảnh khắc nổi bật trên sân cỏ, nam tiền đạo sinh năm 2004 nhiều lần khiến dân tình chú ý. Bùi Hoàng Việt Anh cũng là cái tên được nhắc đến, khiến cuộc bình chọn vui về ngoại hình các cầu thủ càng thêm rôm rả.
Trở lại với Reece, trước khi trở về Việt Nam, Reece từng có quãng thời gian theo đuổi bóng đá ở cả Mỹ, Đức và Thụy Điển. Hành trình này bắt đầu từ khi anh còn là học sinh trung học tại bang Texas (Mỹ). Theo bài viết đăng trên Texarkana Magazine ngày 30/9/2021, Reece khi đó đã có cơ hội sang Đức tham gia chương trình đào tạo bóng đá U19 liên kết với CLB Schalke 04.
Để có được cơ hội này, Reece từng gửi video tổng hợp những tình huống thi đấu nổi bật (highlight) cùng hồ sơ cá nhân để ứng tuyển vào chương trình. Trước đó, anh cũng được lựa chọn vào USYS ODP South Region Pool Team - chương trình tuyển chọn và phát triển cầu thủ trẻ thuộc hệ thống bóng đá trẻ Mỹ. Việc được lựa chọn sang Đức khi vẫn còn ở độ tuổi học sinh là một dấu mốc đáng chú ý trong hành trình theo đuổi bóng đá chuyên nghiệp của cầu thủ Việt kiều.
Sau giai đoạn tại Đức, Reece tiếp tục hành trình ở châu Âu khi gia nhập AFC Eskilstuna (Thụy Điển) vào mùa hè năm 2023 và bắt đầu thi đấu cho đội U19 của CLB. Ngày 27/3/2024, trang thông tin chính thức của AFC Eskilstuna thông báo cầu thủ người Mỹ được đôn lên đội một sau khi gây ấn tượng trong giai đoạn tập huấn trước mùa giải.
Theo chia sẻ từ CLB, Reece đã tập luyện cùng đội một trong suốt giai đoạn chuẩn bị trước mùa giải và góp mặt ở các trận giao hữu. Anh được thử nghiệm ở hành lang cánh phải, trong vai trò hậu vệ phải hoặc tiền vệ cánh phải. Tốc độ và lối chơi giàu năng lượng là những điểm khiến cầu thủ trẻ gây ấn tượng với ban huấn luyện.
Trong phần hỏi đáp được đăng tải trên website đội bóng, khi được đề nghị mô tả về bản thân, Reece cho biết anh là mẫu cầu thủ nhanh nhẹn, linh hoạt và có kỹ thuật.
Anh cũng nhấn mạnh khả năng sử dụng tốc độ để vượt qua hàng phòng ngự đối phương cũng như tham gia pressing tầm cao. Về mục tiêu cá nhân, cầu thủ sinh năm 2004 mong muốn tiếp tục phát triển, tiến bộ hơn cả trong tư cách một cầu thủ lẫn một con người, đồng thời đóng góp vào thành công chung của đội bóng.
Sau thời gian thi đấu tại châu Âu, Reece trở về Việt Nam và gia nhập CLB Bắc Ninh vào cuối tháng 8/2026, hướng đến mùa giải 2026/2027. Đây là cơ hội để tiền vệ Việt kiều tiếp tục tích lũy kinh nghiệm, làm quen với môi trường bóng đá trong nước và tìm kiếm vị trí của mình tại V-League.
Theo thống kê trên hệ thống VPF, Reece đã có tên trong các trận đấu của đội bóng tại mùa giải năm nay, với 2 lần ra sân ở V-League, đều từ băng ghế dự bị.
Không chỉ gây chú ý khi xuất hiện trên sân cỏ, đời sống cá nhân của Reece cũng khiến một bộ phận khán giả tò mò. Trên mạng xã hội Instagram, nam cầu thủ khá kín tiếng, không thường xuyên đăng tải hình ảnh hay chia sẻ quá nhiều về cuộc sống riêng. Dù không hoạt động mạng xã hội quá sôi nổi, Reece vẫn gây ấn tượng nhờ gương mặt sáng, làn da trắng và phong cách trẻ trung.
So với hình ảnh thi đấu trên sân, những khoảnh khắc đời thường của Reece mang đến cảm giác khá giản dị. Anh cũng chưa chia sẻ nhiều về chuyện tình cảm hay các khía cạnh riêng tư khác. Vì vậy, những thông tin được công chúng biết đến hiện chủ yếu vẫn xoay quanh hành trình bóng đá của cầu thủ Việt kiều.

articles.title: This pharmaceutical ETF is outperforming. Why it could keep climbing
articles.text: (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.) Today, we're looking at the Invesco Pharmaceuticals ETF for two reasons: its continued outperformance and how its technical structure provides a useful example of identifying relative strength when scanning for potential trades. The first daily chart, going back to July, shows PJP rallying through the summer, topping in late August, and pulling back into October before advancing again. But zooming out tells a more complete story. The advance actually began in late March and continued through mid-August. The subsequent pullback found support near the 119 to 120 zone, an area that coincided with both prior congestion from July and the 38.2% Fibonacci retracement of the March-to-August advance. These two forms of support suggested a normal pullback within a longer-term uptrend, with buyers stepping in near a key technical area. Another positive has been the tendency for bullish patterns to deliver on their upside targets. Between March and May, PJP formed an inverse head-and-shoulders pattern. The breakout reached its upside target and extended higher, helping fuel a multi-month advance. A similar development occurred in October, when PJP held support and formed another bullish pattern. That formation remains in play, with a potential upside target of 137. The weekly chart provides additional confirmation. PJP has been trending higher since at least 2023, with breakouts to new all-time highs followed by sustained gains in 2024, 2025, and earlier this year. A new breakout would mark the fourth such occurrence. One of the simplest ways to identify relative strength is to scan for stocks or ETFs trading above their 50-day and 200-day moving averages. PJP has spent most of its time above the former and hasn't touched the latter in quite some time. That strength is particularly notable given the broader market. As of Thursday morning, Nov. 5, only 25% of the approximately 170 ETFs we follow were trading above both moving averages. Consider SMH, which spent much of the year above both lines but began deteriorating in July. It has since struggled around its 50-day moving average and recently broke below its 200-day moving average. A scan using these criteria would have excluded SMH while continuing to identify PJP. The bottom line: We want to align ourselves with areas demonstrating relative strength. Successful bullish patterns, support holding during pullbacks, sustained breakouts, and favorable moving-average positioning all help identify potential opportunities. By those measures, PJP continues to stand out, particularly as other areas of the market experience technical deterioration. articles.title: Kỹ sư Nga phát minh tuabin gió hình dáng chưa từng có, được nhà nước cấp luôn bằng sáng chế
articles.text:
Khi đối mặt với bài toán khai thác năng lượng gió tại những vùng hẻo lánh và khắc nghiệt như miền Bắc băng giá hay các khu mỏ vàng xa xôi, rào cản lớn nhất không nằm ở sức gió mà nằm ở chi phí vận chuyển. Việc đưa các cụm máy phát điện công nghiệp nặng hàng tấn và bộ điều tốc đắt đỏ đến những nơi thiếu hụt hạ tầng giao thông luôn là một cơn ác mộng hậu cần.
Xuất phát từ thực tế đó, kỹ sư Valery Fyodorov tại Moscow đã nghĩ phát minh ra một giải pháp táo bạo và đăng ký bản quyền cho một hệ thống điện gió độc đáo. Phát minh này được bảo hộ bởi bằng sáng chế đã được công bố trong cơ sở dữ liệu của Viện Sở hữu Công nghiệp Liên bang Nga (FIPS).
Thay vì trang bị máy phát riêng cho từng tuabin hay tốn tiền mua các hộp số công nghiệp cồng kềnh, ông quyết định tận dụng chính những bộ cầu sau của ô tô thương mại, điển hình như dòng xe Geely Emgrand EC7, để biến chúng thành bộ truyền động hiệu quả.
Ý tưởng cốt lõi của Valery Fyodorov là kết nối sức mạnh của nhiều cánh quạt gió về một máy phát điện duy nhất đặt ngay trên mặt đất. Trong thiết kế này, kỹ sư kết hợp 3 cột trụ gồm hai cột bên và một cột trung tâm cao hơn, tất cả đều tích hợp cơ cấu xoay và nối với nhau bằng dây cáp để có thể tự động xoay chuyển đồng bộ theo hướng gió.
Trên mỗi trụ đặt ít nhất hai động cơ gió, lực quay từ các cánh quạt được gom lại qua hệ thống trục khớp các-đăng (cardan) nối liền thành một chuỗi cơ khí thống nhất.
Điểm bất ngờ nhất nằm ở cách xử lý cầu xe hơi. Kỹ sư Nga đã loại bỏ toàn bộ phần dầm, bán trục, moay-ơ hay phanh trống cồng kềnh, đồng thời thay bộ vi sai bằng một ống nối thép cố định.
Sau khi "gọt giũa", cụm cầu sau trở thành một hộp giảm tốc bánh răng nón gọn nhẹ với tỷ số truyền khoảng 3,9:1. Trọng lượng của cụm chi tiết giảm mạnh từ mức 60–80 kg xuống chỉ còn khoảng 25–35 kg, giúp công đoạn vận chuyển lẫn bảo dưỡng ở những nơi địa hình phức tạp trở nên dễ dàng hơn đáng kể.
Tính linh hoạt của sáng chế này cho phép ghép nối tới 18 cánh quạt gió trên ba trụ máy, dồn toàn bộ cơ năng thu được về một máy phát duy nhất dưới mặt đất qua đường truyền cardan dùng chung.
So với phương án truyền thống phải dùng hộp số công nghiệp hay lắp máy phát riêng trên từng trụ, giải pháp của Valery Fyodorov giúp giảm số chuyến xe vận chuyển vật tư lên tới 85%, mở ra cơ hội cung cấp năng lượng giá rẻ và tự chủ cho những vùng đất xa xôi nhất - bao gồm các vùng phía bắc và các khu khai thác vàng, nơi việc vận chuyển nhiên liệu, hộp số công nghiệp và các linh kiện khác rất tốn kém.
Tham khảo: FT

articles.title: OpenAI will keep investing in AI data centers despite election results, CFO tells CNBC
articles.text:
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar on Friday said the company will continue to invest in artificial intelligence infrastructure, even after voters strongly opposed data centers during Tuesday's midterm elections.
"When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand," Friar told CNBC's Sara Eisen in an interview at the Citi TMT Leadership Summit in Pebble Beach, California. "It starts early with having built relationships with all of the hyperscalers, and it will continue to mean that we raise capital."
Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. Opposition to the facilities mounted swiftly over the summer as Americans grew worried about their potential to harm the environment, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss.
Investors have turned skeptical on the AI trade of late due to a combination of higher borrowing costs, concerns about soaring debt and public backlash toward the industry. The Nasdaq on Thursday suffered its steepest drop in 19 months, led by a plunge in shares of the chipmakers and neocloud companies most closely tied to the AI buildout. The stocks rebounded some on Friday.
OpenAI depends on data centers to train its AI models and serve customers, and Friar said she doesn't think the election results dramatically changed anything for the company. On Thursday, OpenAI published a policy blueprint and a series of commitments that it pledged to apply to company-owned and -operated data centers in the future.
"If the midterm means more focus on data centers and communities, we're going to keep doing the work to get into those communities and to build trust with them," Friar said.
OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, and Friar said Friday that the company would continue to look into a 2027 debut. Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is trying to go public first, with an aim to hit the Nasdaq in mid-November.
Anthropic's revenue in the first nine months of the year jumped roughly 1,200% to $33.2 billion, according to its prospectus. The company said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."
OpenAI is in talks to raise funding at a $1.25 billion pre-money valuation, Friar said Friday. She said "a good CFO always raises money when she can" and that the round is ongoing.
The company has closed an initial $11 billion portion of that funding round, CNBC confirmed on Friday, and it could raise up to an additional $9 billion in the coming weeks. Bloomberg was first to report the $11 billion portion.
"The demand for AI is real," Friar said. "I don't think anyone's arguing with that, or if they are, I think it's a losing argument."
